endorsements.quote: To strengthen oversight and support health and care workers, organisations should establish AI Safety Committees tasked with monitoring, evaluating, and guiding the ethical deployment of AI systems.
Central to this governance is the principle that AI should function as a decision‐support tool, not an autonomous decision‐maker.

Health and care workers must retain ultimate responsibility for decisions informed by AI, with regulatory frameworks reinforcing their role in verifying and validating AI outputs before acting on them.

In addition to governing the data, ethical governance of AI in healthcare must address the critical issue of accountability for AI‐driven decisions, ensuring clear roles and responsibilities across health and care workers, organisations, and AI developers.
Additionally, creating AI registries at the organizational level could enhance accountability by cataloguing AI systems in use, their intended purposes, and performance metrics [ 18 ].
Phased and iterative strategies enable organisations to test, refine and scale AI systems in a controlled manner, reducing the risk of failure.

To avoid biases, AI models should be tested with locally relevant datasets and subjected to regular audits to identify and mitigate inequities, ensuring their effectiveness across diverse patient populations, including for women, men, and other genders.

Central to accountable leadership is proactive engagement with all stakeholders—clinicians, frontline workers, patients and administrators—whose insights are essential to designing and deploying AI systems that work in real‐world settings.
Iterative feedback loops that allow for stakeholder input during deployment and refinement are crucial for ensuring the technology adapts to evolving clinical practices and remains relevant.

Targeted upskilling programs are essential to prepare health and care workers for the changing demands of an AI‐augmented environment, providing them with the technical and adaptive skills necessary to thrive.

unlisted_practices: Involve health and care workers, particularly those from underrepresented groups, in participatory co-design of AI systems.
Embed organizational protections against AI-induced job displacement to guarantee job security for health and care workers.
Develop affordable, context-appropriate AI tools and policies that promote equitable access, including for rural and under-resourced workers.
Adopt transparent and voluntary data collection and sharing practices with informed patients and robust anonymisation to prevent re-identification.
Ensure equitable access to diverse, representative datasets to mitigate bias in AI training data.
Professional regulators should establish policy frameworks that preserve professional autonomy, worker wellbeing and patient-centric care in AI deployment.
Leaders should openly communicate AI capabilities and limitations and avoid overpromising to build trust and realistic expectations.
Maintain human oversight in decision-making processes to guard against over-reliance and erosion of critical thinking and diagnostic skills.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article presenting a framework for responsible AI innovation and governance in healthcare organizations.
